source.title: Small vs. Large Language Models: A Comparative Study on Multiple-Choice Question Answering in Portuguese
source.authors: Marília Rosa Silveira; Guilherme Lima; Carlos Augusto Calage Silveira Júnior; Larissa Astrogildo Freitas; Ulisses Brisolara Corrêa

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some layout is flattened, but the accuracy table and its model/column assignments are clear.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream MCQA accuracy across model sizes, using a task and metric different from held-out pretraining loss, and reports whether performance trends with scale.
record.gate_note: The study reports Portuguese MCQA accuracy by model size and prompting strategy, which bears on V6. It does not measure cross-entropy loss, training tokens or compute, fit scaling exponents, test extrapolation, or find compute-optimal allocations. BPC and answer-position distributions are about positional bias, not a version of the scaling claim, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: It reports Portuguese MCQA accuracy for 11 existing models from 160M to 8B parameters and asks whether accuracy rises with size. That bears on V6 in a new setting (Portuguese exam MCQA). It is an uncontrolled comparison of heterogeneous models: training data, language and instruction tuning differ. No law is fitted and no loss is measured. It is not T1/T2 for the loss-based versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say Kaplan's scaling law 'holds' for Portuguese MCQA, with accuracy rising with parameter count and big gains around 3B and 7–8B. They add that language-specific pretraining (Sabiá vs Bode) matters as much as scale, and that per-option scoring narrows the small–large gap. Larger models are more robust to prompting and position bias, and MCQA alone is not a robust test of knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures Portuguese MCQA accuracy across existing models and prompting strategies, rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss power laws or testing compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompting strategy changes accuracy, particularly for smaller models. The paper reports large differences between ordinary answer-choice prompts and individual-option scoring, as well as different performance among similarly sized models.

fits_no_version.finding: The positional-bias coefficient (BPC) is lower for larger, higher-accuracy models: Sabiá-7B 0.2452 and LLaMA-8B 0.3135, vs TinyLlama 0.9975 and TTL-460m 0.8844. The authors report a negative association between accuracy and BPC.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness to answer-order/positional bias in MCQA improves with model scale.

record.peer_reviewed: Brazilian Symposium on Multimedia and the Web (WebMedia’2025), Proceedings of the Brazilian Symposium on Multimedia and the Web
record.problems: The study compares heterogeneous existing models rather than a controlled size sweep; model training data, language alignment and other characteristics differ. Accuracy is reported as macro-averages across two datasets, with no uncertainty estimates. It measures neither pretraining loss nor a fitted predictive law, and the authors note that MCQA accuracy alone is not a robust validation of knowledge acquisition.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports individual strategy accuracies for all 11 models. To stay within 60 rows while retaining the macro-average for every model and all six strategy results for the models discussed most prominently, individual strategy results 2–5 were omitted for TTL-160m, TTL-460m, Samba-1.1B, Llama-1B and TinyLlama_v1.1. Their macro-averages and strategies 1 and 6 are retained in R01–R11 and R48–R57. BPC and answer-position distribution results are excluded because they concern positional bias rather than a listed scaling-law version.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured; no power-law fits in N, D or C.
Architecture is not varied at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is studied as a scaling law.
Untested: accuracy as a function of pretraining loss, any fitted predictive relationship, and a controlled size sweep within one model family/data recipe (models differ in data, language and tuning).
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The rows mostly hold one model's accuracy with no baseline, so per-row states are not meaningful alone; the V6 evidence lies in comparing rows across sizes. The reader's 'partial' for most small-model rows only reflects near-chance accuracy. Chance is about 20% (five options), which no row states as a baseline. The study is not an original source. Model size is confounded with training data, language focus and instruction tuning. There are no uncertainty estimates and no fitted relationship, so 'predictably' in V6 is only loosely tested. Values checked against Table 1 match.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fits.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
Architecture details are not varied while holding parameter count and other factors fixed.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
The study measures accuracy on Portuguese MCQA, not downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining loss; it does not fit a predictive relationship.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or curve bending. Prompting effects are evaluated, but not as choices in fitting a scaling law.

relationships.condition: Macro-average accuracy over six prompting strategies, across the 11 models (Portuguese ENEM+BLUEX MCQA)
relationships.reason: Sub-2B models score about 22–25% (near chance), LLaMA-3B 36.03%, Sabiá-7B 46.21%, LLaMA-8B 59.44% (R01–R08, R10, R11). This is a broadly rising trend with size, but no fit is made.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy was about 22–25% below 2B parameters, 36.03% for LLaMA-3B, 46.21% for Sabiá-7B, and 59.44% for LLaMA-8B, without a fitted scaling law.

relationships.condition: Models of similar or larger size with different training data/tuning (Bode-7B vs Sabiá-7B and LLaMA-3B)
relationships.reason: Bode-7B (27.71%) is far below Sabiá-7B (46.21%) and below the smaller LLaMA-3B (36.03%), so size alone does not predict accuracy across heterogeneous models (R08, R09, R10).
relationships.display_finding: Bode-7B achieved 27.71%, trailing both Sabiá-7B at 46.21% and the smaller LLaMA-3B at 36.03%.

relationships.reason: Large-model accuracy drops to about 35–40% while small models rise: Tucano-2B reaches 37.12% vs 39.39% for LLaMA-8B and Sabiá-7B, compressing the size gap (R16, R17, R22, R23, R28, R29, R34, R35).
relationships.display_finding: Large-model accuracy fell to roughly 35–40%, while Tucano-2B reached 37.12% versus 39.39% for LLaMA-8B and Sabiá-7B, narrowing the size gap.

relationships.condition: Small models under few-shot / one-shot prompting
relationships.reason: Qwen2-0.5B falls to 12.36% few-shot and 17.54% one-shot, below chance and below smaller TTL models. Prompt choice can swamp size effects at small scale (R24–R26).
relationships.display_finding: Qwen2-0.5B fell below chance to 12.36% with few-shot prompting and 17.54% with one-shot prompting, trailing smaller TTL models.
